evaldesc:
This evaluation checks for the presence of bedrock within a specified depth.  The component data are check for restriction_kind = "bedrock (lithic)" or "bedrock (paralithic)" and restriction_depth_to_top is evaluated.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil component property restriction_kind = "bedrock (lithic)" or "bedrock (paralithic)" and the restriction_depth_to_top is less than 200 then the evaluation is absolutely true and depth to bedrock is a restrictive feature.
     AND
  Where the soil component property restriction_kind = "bedrock (lithic)" or "bedrock (paralithic)" and the restriction_depth_to_top is equla to or greater than 200 cm then the evaluation is absolutely false and depth to bedrock is not a restrictive feature.


Ames Description prior to  1996:

 ___________________________________________________________________
                       |             LIMITS             |RESTRICTIVE
+                       ________________________________
     PROPERTY          |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
                       |          |          |          |
+___________________________________________________________________
 
 7. DEPTH TO BEDROCK       ---        ---        <200     DEPTH TO
    (CM)                                                 ROCK
 
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
 The values given on the Soils-5 for depth to rock are examined and the low value determined.  The low value used for comparison depends on which of the following conditions is met first.
 
 If the low value is valid, then the low value is used.
 
 Otherwise an artificial value of 100 is used.
 
           A value < 200 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A value >= 200 gets a SLIGHT rating.

IMPORTANT: This rule is not designed nor intended to be used in a regulatory manner. It was designed for educational and broad management purposes.

SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil inorganic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SIC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SIC stored in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include sequestered soil inorganic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. 

3. The calculation is reported on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database, the representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil. The soil inorganic carbon is converted from horizon soil inorganic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. 

4. The NPS SIC class rule was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SIC calculated for the component in the NASIS data.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. In these cases the amount of SIC will be underestimated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SIC depending on rock type.

3. If soil inorganic matter in the database is NULL, SIC is assumed to be zero.

evalname: SWM - Filter Field 120 to 200cm 14 to 3.5 um/sec
evaldesc:
7/99 Modification:
This evaluation checks the filtering capacity of the soil.  The maximum high, low, and representative values for sat_hydraulic_conductivity are selected for each horizon between 24 to 72 inches and above any restrictive layer. 

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity > 42 micrometers/second (6.0 inches/hr), the evaluaton is absolutely true and the restrictive feature is poor effluent filter field.
        AND
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity <= 42 micrometers/second (6.0 inches/hour), the evaluation is absolutely false and the restrictive feature is not poor effluent filter field.

If no data is entered, then an artificial default value(s) is used.

In 1990 the evaluation depth was extended from a base of 40 inches to a base of 60 inches.

Ames Description Prior to 1996

                                              |                           LIMITS                              |  RESTRICTIVE
     PROPERTY                 |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
 7. PERMEABILITY          ---                 ---                  >6.0             POOR FILTER
    (IN/HR):    (24-40")            
 
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
   
 The values given on the Soils-5 for permeability are examined and a
 high value for each layer is determined.  The high value used for
 comparison depends on which of the following conditions is met
 first.
 
 If no data is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used.
 
 If the entry is a single number or is of the form '<xx', then the
  single value entered is used.
 
 If the entry is of the form '>xx', then an artificial value of 100
  is used.
 
 Otherwise the high value is used.
 
 The layers within the given depths are examined.  If surface layers are included in these depths, each is rated separately.  Then each sublayer is rated to determine the worst sublayer rating.  The rating algorithm used on each layer is as follows:
 
           A value > 6.0 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A value <= 6.0 gets a SLIGHT rating.
 
 If surface layers are not involved, then this property is rated the
 same as the worst sublayer rating.
 
 If surface layers are involved, then the following applies.  If the
 worst sublayer rating is SEVERE, then this property is rated SEVERE
 and no phasing will be done, regardless of the surface layer
 ratings.
 
 If the worst sublayer rating is SLIGHT, then this property is rated
 SLIGHT if there is any SLIGHT surface layer rating, and it is rated
 SEVERE if there is any SEVERE surface layer rating.  Phasing will be
 done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.
propname: KSAT HIGHEST MIN ABOVE RESTR, BELOW O, 120 TO 200 CM

Dissolution of bone minerals is closely related to pH.  Dissolution is much faster in an acidic environment.  The potential of a soil to tend to preserve bones is to some extent a function of pH.  The actual pH in the vicinity of the bones would be difficult to determine.  The pH of the surrounding soil, with mixing during burial, can be estimated.

It is absolutely true that if the soil pH around bones is greater than 6.5, bones will be preserved, while at pH below 5.3, the statement is absolutely false.

Likelihood of bone preservation high	pH >6.5
Some likelihood of bone preservation	pH 5.3 to 6.5
Little likelihood of bone preservation	pH <5.3

It is absolutely true, extremely wet soil conditions promote bone preservation.

Evaluates SOC to a depth of two meter or to the occurrence of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 

SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stored in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include sequestered soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation is reported on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database, the representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. 

4. The NPS SOC class rule was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. In these cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type.

3. An alternative script could be written to use the horizon rock fragment volume instead of sieves if sieves are NULL. At present, when the #10 sieves are null 100% passing is the default.

4. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

Soil Particle Size
Research has shown that the growth of hard clams is dependent on the soil type. Although hard clams inhabit a variety of soil types, clams grew fifty percent faster in sand than mud in Great South Bay, New York (Greene, 1975) and clams grew twenty four percent faster in sand than mud in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island (Pratt, 1953). A study done by Salisbury (2010) found that quahog growth rates increased and mortality rates decreased on coarse textured subaqueous soils. There was also a high correlation between shell length and substrate particle size in Little Bay, New Jersey (Johnson, 1977).

Hard clams have been found to prefer sediments that are coarse yet firm, with complex surface topography that may include shell fragments (Kassner et al. 1991; Murphy and Erkan 2006). Kassner et al. (1991) found that muddy sediments (soils) are less preferable, as much as a seven-fold increase in clam abundance in sandy substrates with shell fragments compared to muddy sediments. The authors also found the highest clam abundances in sediments that were coarse yet firm, not highly reworked (by other benthic organisms), had complex surface topography with a high degree of shell fragments. Keck et al. (1974) found that significantly higher numbers of hard clams set in sand than in mud. Carriker (1959) recommended that the substrate be firm and free of excessive organic mud. Other studies have shown that hard clams are more likely to live on a sandy bottom than on a mud bottom (Allen, 1954; Maurer and Watling, 1973; Mitchell, 1974). Rice and Pechenick (1992) found that hard clam growth increased in sand, a sediment type indicative of higher flow velocities and a more rapid resupply of food. 

Some evidence suggests that hard clams grow slower in finer, muddy sediments than in coarser, sandy sediments (Pratt 1953). Pratt and Campbell (1956) suggested that one explanation for this depressed growth rate was the tendency of finer sediments to be less oxygenated and to contain more sulfide than coarser sediments. Kassner et al. (1991) found the lowest clam abundance in clay and mud sediments. As the percentage of fine textured soil particles (silt and clay) increases, clams must more frequently clear their filtering apparatus, which expends more energy and limits feeding thus decreasing growth. In Figure 6, the graph shows that as the percentage of percent silt and clay in soil increases the suitability of hard clam habitat decreases (Mulholland, 1984).

evalname: Depth to Petrocalcic Horizon 0 to 100cm (TX) orig
evaldesc:
This evaluation checks the depth to a petrocalcic hoizon and indexes the degree to which depth is limiting.  Where the soil property "DEPTH TO PETROCALCIC (TX)" is:
	       = 0cm  the soil is a potential source of caliche and the potential index is expressed as the number 0.0.
	       > 0cm and <= 100cm the soil is a potential source of caliche and the potential index is expressed as anumber between 0 and 1.0.
	       > 100cm the soil is not a potential source of caliche and the potential index is expressed as the number 1.0.

evalname: Thickness of Petrocalcic Horizon 10 to 50cm (TX) orig
evaldesc:
This evaluation checks the thickness of the caliche layer and indexes the degree to which thickness is limiting.  Where the soil property "THICKNESS OF PETROCALCIC ABOVE BEDROCK OR 100CM  (TX)" is:

	   > = 50cm  the soil is a potential source of caliche and the potential index is expressed as the number 0.0.
	      > 10cm and < 50cm the soil is a potential source of caliche and the potential index is expressed as anumber between 0 and 1.0.
	   >= 10cm the soil is not a potential source of caliche and the potential index is expressed as the number 1.0.
propname: THICKNESS OF PETROCALCIC ABOVE BEDROCK OR 100CM  (TX)

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks soil's taxonomic moisture classification and indexes the degree to which the soil taxonomic moisture is limiting.  Where the soil property "TAXONOMIC SUBGROUP (TX)" matches:

	else the soil is not member of the group and the degree of membership is expressed as the number 0.

	else the soil is not member of the group and the degree of membership is expressed as the number 0.

This evaluation checks the USDA texture of the soil horizon between 50 and 180cm and indexes the degree to which the texture is limiting.  Where the soil property "USDA TEXTURE SILT LOAM IN DEPTH 50-180cm (TX)" matches:

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks the Organic Matter to Clay relationship where if OM <= (8+(claytotal_r/7.5) then the relationship is true else false.  If the relationship is false then the soils have OM matter contents that are to high.  Where the soil property "ORGANIC MATTER TO CLAY RELATIONSHIP 0-180CM-OSHA (TX)" matches:
	    
	= 1 the soil does not have high organic matter content and the degree of membership is expressed as the number 1.0.
	= 0 the soil has high organic matter content and the degree of membership is expressed as the number 0.0.

	   > 15% the soil is limited and the index is expressed as the number 0.

evalname: TN Septic - Wet, Apparent Ground Water
evaldesc:
This evaluation checks for an apparent saturated or wet condition between a depth of 60 to 150 cm (2 to 5 feet) of the soil surface.  The water moisture status for all layers are examined and those saturated or wet layers are evalutated for depth.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where soil_moisture_status is wet and the depth to soil_moist_depth_to_top is less than 150 cm (5 feet) the evaluation is absolutely false and DEEP TO WATER is not a restrictive feature.
   OR
  Where soil_moisture_status is wet and the depth to  soil_moist_depth_to_top  is greater than >= 150 cm (5 feet) the evaluation is absolutely true and DEEP TO WATER is a restrictive feature.

If the soil_moisture_status is not wet or null, then the property asumption is that soil_moist_depth_to_top is NULL and no water table is present.

Ames Description Prior to 1996:
1___________________________________________________________________
                       |             LIMITS             |RESTRICTIVE
+                       ________________________________
     PROPERTY          |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
                       |          |          |          |
+___________________________________________________________________

 2. DEPTH TO HIGH
    WATER TABLE (FT):
    APPARENT                <2
                                      2-5                DEEP TO
                                                         WATER
                                                25/>5    NO WATER

    PERCHED                                     25/ANY   NO WATER
                                                ENTRY

 25/If NO WATER, disregard other properties.



 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________

 The low value in the range of values given on the Soils-5 for depth
 to high water table is examined.  The value used for comparison
 depends on which of the following conditions is met first.

 If no data is entered, then an artificial value of 99.9 is used.

 Otherwise the low value is used.

 If the water table kind is not perched, then the following ratings
 apply:
           A value >= 5 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A value >= 2 and < 5 gets a MODERATE rating.
           A value < 2 gets a SLIGHT rating.

 If a SEVERE rating is given, then no other properties in this guide
 are rated.

 If the water table kind is perched, then no other properties in
 this guide are rated.
propname: TN - SEPTIC DEPTH TO HIGH WATER TABLE APPARENT MINIMUM

evalname: TN Septic - Wet, Ground Water Perched
evaldesc:
This evaluation checks for a perched saturated or wet condition within a depth of 120 cm (4 feet) of the soil surface.  The water moisture status for all layers are examined and those saturated or wet layers are evalutated for depth.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where soil_moisture_status is wet, has a dry layer below the wet layer, and the depth to soil_moist_depth_to_top is less than 50 cm the evaluation is absolutely true and WETNESS is a restrictive feature.
   OR
  Where soil_moisture_status is wet, has a dry layer below the wet layer, and the depth to  soil_moist_depth_to_top  is greater than >= 100  cm) the evaluation is absolutely false and WETNESS is a restrictive feature.

If the soil_moisture_status is not wet or null, then the property asumption is that soil_moist_depth_to_top is NULL and no water table is present.

Prior to 1996
                                                |                           LIMITS                              |   RESTRICTIVE
     PROPERTY                   |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
 6. DEPTH TO HIGH                >3                  1.5-3                <1.5           WETNESS
    WATER TABLE (FT):
        PERCHED

 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________

 The water table kind and the low value in the range of values given
 on the Soils-5 for depth to high water table are examined.  If a '+'
 occurs in the low value, then there is ponding and a SEVERE rating
 is given.  Otherwise the value used for comparison depends on which
 of the following conditions is met first.

 If no data is entered, then an artificial value of 99.9 is used.

 Otherwise the low value is used.

 If the water table kind is perched, then the following ratings apply:
           A value < 1.5 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A value >= 1.5 and < 3 gets a MODERATE rating.
           A value >= 3 gets a SLIGHT rating.
propname: TN - SEPTIC DEPTH TO HIGH WATER TABLE PERCHED MINIMUM

A soil scores a one if the bulk density of its horizons are the same as the "ideal" for its constituent make-up.  The lowest a soil can score is a 0.5, if it is twice as dense as the ideal (this probably never happens).  The weighted average of the horizons above a restrictive layer is examined by this evaluation.

It is thought that very few soils can get a score of 1, thus, the upper scores will have some spread such that differences can be seen.

Where the soil property "DEPTH TO HIGH WATER TABLE MIN DURING GROWING SEASON (ND)" is:

	>= 25 and <= 75 cm                        the soil is limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 1.0.
    > 20 and < 25 cm OR > 75 AND < 100 cm   the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation is expressed a number between 0 and 1.0. 
	<= 20 OR >= 100 cm                       the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 0.

Logic: 
Risk of salinization on well drained soils is low, and on moderately well to poorly drained soils, it is proportionately higher. Accumulation of salts is more likely in soils where the soil surface is actually the evaporative surface. Very poorly drained soils are ranked with a lower risk, because of their high degree of saturation and persistence of surface wetness. Evaporation from a water surface does not actually leave salts in the soil.

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

Reference:
Eilers, R.G., Eilers, W.D., Fitzgerald, M.M., 1997, A Salinity Risk Index for Soils of the Canadian Prairies : Hydrology Journal, v. 5, no. 1, p. 68-79.

Anderson, K., Zimmerman, D., Ulmer, M., 2010, Development and Application of a Salinity Risk Index for the Red River Valley of the North, MLRA 56.

The evaluation checks rock fragments greater then 10 inches on the soil surface and indexes the degree to which of LARGE STONES limits the suitability for use.  Where the soil property "FRAGMENTS >=250MM ON THE SURFACE" is:

	 => 50 the soil is not suited and the degree of suitability is expressed as the number 0.
	  > 0 and < 50 the soil is somewhat suited and the degree of suitability is expressed as a number between 0 and 1.0.
	 = 0 the soil is suited and the degree of suitability is expressed as the number 1.0.

This evaluation checks the soil's bulk density within a depth of 0 to 150 cm and indexes the degree to which bulk density is limiting.  
Where the soil property "BULK DENSITY MAXIMUM IN DEPTH 0-150CM (ND)" is:
	 >=    1.8                  the soil is limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 1.0.
  	 >=    1.5 and < 1.8 the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as a number between 0 and 1.0.
	 <       1.5                  the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

This evaluation checks for total subsidence and indexes the degree that total subsidence is limiting.
Where the soil property "SUBSIDENCE TOTAL (ND)" is:
     >= 30 cm             the soil is limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 1.0.
     > 0 and < 30 cm  the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as a number between 0 and 1.0.
     0                           the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

evaldesc:

     > 0.01 and <0.1%       the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as a number between 0 and 1.0.
     <= 0.01%                     the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

     >= 1.0 um/sec              the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

     >= 15            the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

Where bulk_density_one_third_bar is greater then 1.8 for any layer within a depth of 50 to 150 cm (20 to 60 inches) the evaluation is true and the restrictive feature is DENSE LAYER.  However, this restriction has only a moderate inpact on the interpretation.

 7. BULK DENSITY (G/CC)    	     ---                  >1.8                   ---            DENSE LAYER
    (20-60")

 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
 The values given on the Soils-5 for bulk density are examined.  A high value is determined for each layer within 20-60 inches depending on which of the following conditions is met first.
 
 If the entry is a normal range, then the high value is used.
 
 If the entry is of the form '>xx', then an artificial value of 99.99 is used.
 
 If the entry is a single number or is of the form '<xx', then the single value entered is used.
 
 Otherwise an artificial value of 0 is used.
 
 If any of the determined values is > 1.8, then this property is rated SEVERE.  Otherwise it is rated SLIGHT.

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks the soil's aluminium saturation to a depth of 0 to 10cm or a restrictive layer and indexes the degree to which the soil's aluminium saturation is contributes to the soil's plant growth potential.  Where the soil property "ALUMINIUM SATURATION HORIZON DEPTH <10cm" is:

AL SATURATION
		

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

 Description of Calculation for Thickest Layer:
+______________________________________________

 The layer with the most inches between 10 and 60 inches is determined.  This could be a surface layer or a sublayer.  The unified values given on the Soils-5 are examined for the appropriate layer(s).

 The layer(s) being examined are rated according to the following algorithm:

 If GW, GP, GW-GM, or GP-GM is listed as a unified entry, or if SW, SP, SW-SM or SP-SM is listed as a unified entry and footnote 15 applies (see following description of footnote 15), then a PROBABLE rating is given.

 Otherwise an IMPROBABLE rating is given.

 If the thickest layer is a sublayer, then this property is rated the same as this sublayer's rating.

 If the thickest layer is a surface layer, then this property is rated PROBABLE if there is any PROBABLE surface layer rating.  If there is none, then it is rated IMPROBABLE.

 Restrictive feature terms are assigned appropriately.



 Description of Calculation for Bottom Layer:
+____________________________________________

 If the bottom layer has no data, then this calculation is skipped and the ratings for the thickest layer are chosen.

 Otherwise, this calculation is the same as that for the thickest layer, except it is done for the bottom layer.  The bottom layer,
 like the thickest layer, may be a surface layer or a sublayer.

 Calculations for Footnotes 15 and 16
+____________________________________

 To do the calculations for these footnotes, the values given on the Soils-5 for % passing No. 4 sieve are examined.

 % passing No. 4 sieve
+_____________________

 Assign values to No_4_Lo and No_4_Hi.

 If no data is entered, then No_4_Lo = 0 and No_4_Hi = 0.

 If a single value, say x, is entered, then No_4_Lo = x and  No_4_Hi = x.

 If the entry is a normal range, say x-y, then No_4_Lo = x and  No_4_Hi = y.

 Once these values have been assigned, the following calculations take place.

 100 - No_4_Lo = Lo
 100 - No_4_Hi = Hi

 maximum(Lo,Hi) = max

 If max > 25 then footnote 15 applies.
 If max <= 25 then footnote 16 applies.

 For Property No. 2, UNIFIED, the best ratings must be chosen between those calculated for the thickest layer and the bottom layer.

 If both the thickest and bottom layers are rated PROBABLE, then the bottom layer is chosen.

 If the thickest layer is rated PROBABLE and the bottom layer is rated IMPROBABLE, then the thickest layer is chosen.

 If the bottom layer is rated PROBABLE and the thickest layer is rated IMPROBABLE, then the bottom layer is chosen.

 If neither the thickest or bottom layer is rated PROBABLE, then they must both be rated IMPROBABLE and the bottom layer is chosen.

 If the ratings for the thickest layer were chosen, then the calculations on the following page for Property No. 3, LAYER
 THICKNESS, are done.

evaldesc:
This evaluation is looking at the map unit name where it has any portion of the name being Rock outcrop, rocky or very rocky.

The evaluation is an arbitrary linear line that evaluates the map unit name where anything that had Rock outcrop in the name is out of the class and returns a value of 1. Any map unit with "rocky" in the name is a partial member of the class and is given a fuzzy value of 0.3. Any map unit with "very rocky" in the name is also a parital member of the class and is given a fuzzy value of 0.7. Any map unit that does not include these words in their name is considered a member of the class and returns a value of 0.

This evaluation checks aashto_group_index.  The component data are check for aashto_group_index index number.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil component property aashto_group_index is greater than 16 then the evaluation is absolutely true and LOW STRENGTH is a restrictive feature.
     AND
  Where the soil component property aashto_group_index is less then 5 then the evaluation is absolutely false and LOW STRENGTH is not a restrictive feature.


Ames Description prior to  1996:
____________________________________________________________________
                                                             |             LIMITS                                              |RESTRICTIVE
+                                                         ________________________________
     PROPERTY                              |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE     |  FEATURE
 +___________________________________________________________________
 
 6. 5/, 9/, 10/AASHTO                     <5                   4-16                        >16               LOW  STRENGTH
    GROUP INDEX NUMBER                                   
    
 5/If in Kaolinitic family, rate one class better if experience confirms.
 9/Thickest layer between 10 and 40 inches.
 10/GIN=(F-35)[.2+.005(LL-40)]+.01(F-15)(PI-10) where F=% passing No. 200 sieve.  If F<=35 and PI>=11, use only part 2 of equation.  Use median values.
 
 
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
 The layer with the most inches between 0 and 16 inches is determined.  This could be a surface layer or a sublayer.  The GIN is calculated for the appropriate layer(s) according to the given algorithm.
 
 To calculate the GIN, median values are needed for the following: percent passing No. 200 sieve (F), liquid limit (LL), and plasticity index (PI).  A median is calculated by adding the low and high values, then dividing by 2, unless special conditions exist.  The median calculation is given below for each of these three variables.
 
 Percent passing No. 200 sieve:
+______________________________
 
 If no valid data is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used as the median.
 
 If a single value is entered, then this value is used as the median.
 
 Otherwise the median is calculated using the low and high values.
 

 
 Liquid limit:
+_____________
 
 If the entry is of the form '<xxx', then a median is calculated using 0 and xxx. 
 If the entry is of the form '>xxx', then a median is calculated using xxx and 100.
  If no valid data is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used as the median. 
 If a single value is entered, then this value is used as the median. 
 Otherwise the median is calculated using the low and high values.
 
 Plasticity index:
+_________________
 
 If the entry is of the form '<xxx', then a median is calculated using 0 and xxx. 
 If the entry is of the form '>xxx', then a median is calculated using xxx and 100. 
 If the entry is of the form 'NP', then an artificial value of 0 is used as the median. 
 
 If the entry is of the form 'NP-xxx', then a median is calculated using 0 and xxx. 
 If no valid data is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used as the median. 
 If a single value is entered, then this value is used as the median. 
 Otherwise the median is calculated using the low and high values. 
 After the GIN is calculated, the layer(s) being examined are rated according to the following algorithm: 
    If GIN > 16, then a SEVERE rating is given.
    If GIN > 5 and <= 16, then a MODERATE rating is given.
    If GIN <= 5, then a SLIGHT rating is given.
 
 If the thickest layer is a sublayer, then this property is rated the same as this sublayer's rating.  If mineralogy on the Soils-5 equals '28' (Kaolinitic), then a MODERATE rating is upgraded to SLIGHT, and a SEVERE rating is upgraded to MODERATE.
 
 If the thickest layer is a surface layer, then this property is rated SLIGHT if there is any SLIGHT surface layer rating, MODERATE if there is any MODERATE surface layer rating, and SEVERE if there is any SEVERE surface layer rating.  If mineralogy on the Soils-5 equals '28' (Kaolinitic), then a MODERATE rating is upgraded to SLIGHT, and a SEVERE rating is upgraded to MODERATE.  Phasing will be done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.
propname: aashto GROUP INDEX, THICKEST LAYER IN DEPTH 0-41cm (WV)

7/99 Modification:
This evaluation checks the filtering capacity of the soil.  The maximum high, low, and representative values for sat_hydraulic_conductivity are selected for each horizon between 24 to 72 inches and above any restrictive layer. 

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity > 42 micrometers/second (6.0 inches/hr), the evaluaton is absolutely true and the restrictive feature is poor effluent filter field.
        AND
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity <= 42 micrometers/second (6.0 inches/hour), the evaluation is absolutely false and the restrictive feature is not poor effluent filter field.

If no data is entered, then an artificial default value(s) is used.

In 1990 the evaluation depth was extended from a base of 40 inches to a base of 60 inches.

Ames Description Prior to 1996

                                              |                           LIMITS                              |  RESTRICTIVE
     PROPERTY                 |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
 7. PERMEABILITY          ---                 ---                  >6.0             POOR FILTER
    (IN/HR):    (24-40")            
 
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
   
 The values given on the Soils-5 for permeability are examined and a
 high value for each layer is determined.  The high value used for
 comparison depends on which of the following conditions is met
 first.
 
 If no data is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used.
 
 If the entry is a single number or is of the form '<xx', then the
  single value entered is used.
 
 If the entry is of the form '>xx', then an artificial value of 100
  is used.
 
 Otherwise the high value is used.
 
 The layers within the given depths are examined.  If surface layers are included in these depths, each is rated separately.  Then each sublayer is rated to determine the worst sublayer rating.  The rating algorithm used on each layer is as follows:
 
           A value > 6.0 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A value <= 6.0 gets a SLIGHT rating.
 
 If surface layers are not involved, then this property is rated the
 same as the worst sublayer rating.
 
 If surface layers are involved, then the following applies.  If the
 worst sublayer rating is SEVERE, then this property is rated SEVERE
 and no phasing will be done, regardless of the surface layer
 ratings.
 
 If the worst sublayer rating is SLIGHT, then this property is rated
 SLIGHT if there is any SLIGHT surface layer rating, and it is rated
 SEVERE if there is any SEVERE surface layer rating.  Phasing will be
 done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.
propname: KSAT MAX RV, 24 to 80" 60-200CM, OR FIRST RESTRICTIONPRF

evaldesc:
This evaluation check percolation capacity of the soil.  The high, low, and representative values for sat_hydraulic_conductivity are selected for each horizon between 24 to 72 inches. 

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity < 4.0 micrometers/second (0.60 inches/hour)the evaluation is absolutely true and the restrictive feature is slow percolation.
        AND
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity => 14.0 micrometers/second (2.00 inches/hour) the evaluation is absolutely false and the restrictive feature is not slow percolation.

If no data is entered, then an artificial default value(s) is used. 

Ames Description Prior to 1996:
                                                   |                           LIMITS                              |   RESTRICTIVE
     PROPERTY                      |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
 7. PERMEABILITY              2.0-6.0          I/0.6-2.0               <0.6         PERCS SLOWLY
    (IN/HR):    (24-60")            

    I/Recheck to see if rating should be SLIGHT.

 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
 This property is calculated as if it were two separate properties.
 The calculation for the first line (PERCS SLOWLY) is:
 
 The values given on the Soils-5 for permeability are examined and a
 low value for each layer is determined.  The low value used for
 comparison depends on which of the following conditions is met
 first.
 
 If no data is entered, then an artificial value of 100 is used.
 
 If the entry is of the form '<xx', then an artificial value of 0 is
  used.
 
 Otherwise the low value is used.
 
 The layers within the given depths are examined.  If surface layers
 are included in these depths, each is rated separately.  Then each
 sublayer is rated to determine the worst sublayer rating.  The
 rating algorithm used on each layer is as follows:

           A value < 0.6 gets a SEVERE rating
           A value >= 0.6 and < 2.0 gets a MODERATE rating.
           A value >= 2.0 gets a SLIGHT rating.
 
 If surface layers are not involved, then this property is rated the
 same as the worst sublayer rating.
 
 If surface layers are involved, then the following applies.  If the
 worst sublayer rating is SEVERE, then this property is rated SEVERE
 and no phasing will be done, regardless of the surface layer
 ratings.
 
 If the worst sublayer rating is MODERATE, then this property is
 rated MODERATE if there is any SLIGHT or MODERATE surface layer
 rating, and it is rated SEVERE if there is any SEVERE surface layer
 rating.  Phasing will be done using texture terms if more than one
 rating is given.
 
 If the worst sublayer rating is SLIGHT, then this property is rated
 SLIGHT if there is any SLIGHT surface layer rating, MODERATE if
 there is any MODERATE surface layer rating, and SEVERE if there is
 any SEVERE surface layer rating.  Phasing will be done using texture
 terms if more than one rating is given.
propname: KSAT MIN RV, 24 to 80" 60-200CM, OR FIRST RESTRICTIONPRF

evaldesc:
11/256/2008 Edited low pH in trapezoid to 3.0, from 3.5 and high was 10.0, was edited to be 11.0 

Evaluates the lowest pH in depth 0-25 cm below any organic duff horizons

The fuzzy space is defined as:

If the soil profile pH is greater than 5.5 and less than 8.5 then the soil surface is optimum for plant growth and the evaluation is nearly true.  Thus, slightly acid surface layers are optimal for plant growth but medium acid and neutral soils are also well suited for supporting plant growth.

If the soil profile pH is less than 5.5 or greater than 8.5 then the soil surface pH is not optimal for plant growth.  When the pH of the soil surface is more acid or alkaline then the optimum pH range, reduced availability of nutrients and the affects of heavy metals and salt concentrations limit plant growth.

Reference:
1. Nyles C Brady, Weil.  The Nature and Properties of Soils, Twelfth Edition. 1999. pp. 593-607
2. Agronomic Interpretations Working Group. 1995. Land Suitability Rating System for Agricultural Crops; 1. Spring-seeded small grains.  Editied by W.W. Pettapiece. Tech. Bull. 1995-6E.. Center for Land and Biological Resources Research, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Ottawa. pp. 17.

evaldesc:
This evaluation evaluates the product of the shrink-swell value of the thickest horizon in the 0 to 50cm range.

If the shrink-swell value for the thickest layer between 0-50cm is between 3 and 6, the evaluation returns a value between 0 and 1.

When the shrink-swell value for the thickest layer between 0 to 50cm is > 6 (HIGH or VERY HIGH) the evaluation is absolutely true and the restrictive feature is SHRINK-SWELL.

A soil may be a full member, partial member, or non-member of the set of soils in which the inherent productivity is not limited by rock fragment content.  The major effect of rock fragment content, that of diluting the soil and lowering the water and nutrient holding capacities, are accounted for in the AWC and MEQ calculations.  The remaining effect is that of the energy expended by the plant in trying to get around the rocks to find water and nutrients.

CEC is handled in a manner analogous to AWC.  The amount of exchange for each layer is calculated, adjusted for density, and reduced for any rock fragment content.  The exchage amounts for each layer are then summed for all layers above excessively high electrical conductivity.

A soil having a capacity of 50 meq or higher gets a score of 1, a soil having a capacity of 5 or less gets a score of 0.2.

CEC is handled in a manner analogous to AWC.  The amount of exchange for each layer is calculated, adjusted for density, and reduced for any rock fragment content.  The exchage amounts for each layer are then summed for all layers above a restrictive layer.

A soil having a capacity of 50 meq or higher gets a score of 1, a soil having a capacity of 5 or less gets a score of 0.2.

CEC is handled in a manner analogous to AWC.  The amount of exchange for each layer is calculated, adjusted for density, and reduced for any rock fragment content.  The exchage amounts for each layer are then summed for all layers above excessively low pH (<3.5).

A soil having a capacity of 50 meq or higher gets a score of 1, a soil having a capacity of 5 or less gets a score of 0.2.

This evaluation checks the available water of the soil.  The total avialable water is calculated for the soil and the result is check and evaluated.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
 
  Where the total available water to a depth of 150cm (60in) is less than 7.5 cm (3 in) the evaluation is absolutely true and "DROUGHTY" is a restrictive feature.
     AND
  Where the total avaiilable water to a depth of 150cm (60in) is greater than 15 cm (6 in) the evaluation is absolutely false and "DROUGHTY" is not a restrictive feature.

Ames Description prior to  1996:
 ___________________________________________________________________
                       |             LIMITS             |RESTRICTIVE
+                       ________________________________
     PROPERTY          |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
                       |          |          |          |
+___________________________________________________________________
 
 14. AVAILABLE WATER        >6        3-6         <3     DROUGHTY
     (WEIGHT AVE, 0 TO 60")
  
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
 The values given on the Soils-5 for available water are examined and
 
 If no data is entered, then the layer is skipped.
 
 If the entry is a single number, then the single value entered is used as the average.
 
 If the entry is of the form '<xxxx', then the average is taken using 0 and xxxx.
 
 Otherwise the low value is used.
 
 
 A separate total is calculated for each surface layer and then rated.  The total is the sum of each layer's average value times the number of inches in the layer for layers up to 60".
 
           A value < 3 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A value >= 3 and < 6 gets a MODERATE rating.
           A value >= 6 gets a SLIGHT rating.
 
 If there is a value rated SEVERE, then this property is rated SEVERE.  If there is a value rated MODERATE, then this property is rated MODERATE.  If there is a value rated SLIGHT, then this property is rated SLIGHT.  Phasing will be done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.

evaldesc:
The scoring curve for soil organic matter content in the surface layer ("A" or "O" horizon) is based on the curve developed by the Cornell soil health assessment (medium curve). This was chosen because of the high inherent organic matter contents of the northeast (based on climate and soils), and would provide the maximum potential for organic matter and soil quality on agricultural soils (of that found within the US). The organic matter content ranges from 0 to 7% with a score of one as the most limiting with zero percent organic matter. Anything over 7% gets a score of zero. 

The scoring curve shape is sigmoid as follows:

          Organic Matter score = (a + cx + ex2)/(1 + bx + dx2 +fx3)
          a = 1.0002993; b = -0.14767395; c = -0.21024973; d = -0.0081101367; e = 0.009697; f = 0.0073572721; x = organic matter (%)

evalname: Rooting Depth to First Restriction or 152 cm
evaldesc:
The scoring curve for effective rooting depth is developed based a maximum depth of 152 cm as being the least vulnerable to soil erosion. Response of crop yield to erosion is generally convex (Bakker et al., 2004). As erosion continues and the soil gets shallower increasingly severe productivity losses occur under equal erosion rates. The curve is based on depth to a root restrictive layer or 152 cm, whichever is shallower. 

The following is the scoring curve:

          Rooting Depth Score = a + bx + cx1.5 + dx3 
          a = 1.0000338; b = -0.019773028; c = 0.0011661322; d = -5.1038528e-08; x = rooting depth (cm)

The scoring curve for vegetative cover is based on the percent cover assigned to each earth-cover-kind 1 and 2 ( plus any surface fragment cover) for a component. Vegetative cover plus surface fragment cover can range from 0 to 100%.

The De Martonne (1926) aridity index (Am) (as reviewed in Maliva and Missimer, 2012 and Lunga et al., 2011) uses temperature as a proxy for ETp as follows: Am = P/(T + 10) where, P (mm) is the annual precipitation and T (C) the annual mean temperature. The equation is appropriate for temperatures greater than -9.9C. The De Martonne aridity index decreases (approaches zero) with increasing aridity. Aridity index values greater the 30 are considered not fragile.

The shape of the scoring curve is sigmoid as follows:

	Aridity Index score = (a + cx + ex2)/(1 + bx + dx2)
	a = 0.99992575; b = -0.069544299; c = -0.065093715; d = 0.0019192058; e = 0.0010584767; x = aridity index

The equation is appropriate for temperatures greater than -9.9C. The De Martonne aridity index decreases (approaches zero) with increasing aridity. Aridity index values greater the 30 are considered not fragile.

The shape of the scoring curve is sigmoid as follows:

The scoring curve is based on the structure classes developed by Bob Grossman. The type, grade and size of structural units are grouped into classes as defined in Table 3 of the soil quality morphology index (Seybold et al., 2004). Structure classes range from 1 to 5 with 5 being the best. Scores are as follows:
	
Structure Class score= 1 if structure class 1; 0.75 if structure class 2; 0.5 if structure class 3; 0.25 if structure class 4; 0 if structure class 5

When high quality water (e.g., rain or snow water) is used, an ESP of 5 can be detrimental to the physical properties of soils. When waters of higher salinities are used (>3 meq/L), only ESP values higher than 15 will cause soil damage. Shainberg and Letey (1983)

An organic matter to clay ratio percent > 7%  is considered to have a favourable influence on structural stability (Valentin, 1989). Stability increases for the same organic mater content in sandy soil than in clayey soils.

A soil organic carbon to clay ratio of 1:10 (organic carbon*1.72/10 x 100 = 17.2%) was considered the limit between good and medium structrual quality (Johannes et al., 2017).

The soil organic carbon to clay ratio decreases with decreasing soil structural stability (Johannes et al., 2017). A soil organic carbon to clay ratio of 1:8 is the average for a very good structure quality (organic carbon*1.72/8*100 = 21.5%).

evaldesc:
The clay dispersion ratio was found to be a good index for predicting the erodibility of soils of southeastern Nigeria (Igwe, 2005).

The dispersion ratio (silt + clay in suspension/(total silt + clay)) was shown to be the single most valuable criterion in distinguishing between erosive and nonerosive soils (Middleton, 1930). It was suggested that a dispersion ratio of less than 0.15 can be considered nonerosive.

Soils low in clay (%) and in SOM(%) content and high in silt (%) content are highly prone to sealing and crusting. CI < 0.2 indicates no crust
formation and a value > 2 is considered a critical limit for high crust formation risk.

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks for coarse fragments greater than 10 inches in the soil surface.  The rock_frag_greater_than_10_in is check and evaluated.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
 
  Where the result of the soil component surface horizon property rock_frag_greater_than_10_in is greater than 15 percent by weight the evaluation is absolutely true and "TOO STONY" is a restrictive feature.
     AND

                       |          |          |          |
+___________________________________________________________________
 
 13b. WEIGHT PERCENT >10"   <5         5-15       >15    TOO STONY
      (SURFACE LAYER)
  
 Description of Calculation:
 
The values given on the Soils-5 for fraction >10 inches are examined and a high value for each layer is determined.  The high value used in the calculation depends on which of the following conditions is met first.
 
 If a single value of '99' is entered, then an artificial value of 100 is used.
 
 If a single value not equal to '99' is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used.
 
 Otherwise the high value is used.
 
 A separate weighted average is calculated for each surface layer.
 
       A weighted average > 15 gets a SEVERE rating.
       A weighted average > 5 and <= 15 gets a MODERATE rating.
       A weighted average <= 5 gets a SLIGHT rating.
 
 Phasing will be done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks the filtering capacity of the soil.  The minimum high, low, and representative values for  sat_hydraulic_conductivity are selected to a depth of 60 inches. 

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity >= 42 micrometers/second (6.0 inches/hr), the evaluaton is absolutely true and the restrictive feature is poor effulent filter field.
        AND
  Where the soil horizon property sat_hydraulic_conductivity <= 14 micrometers/second (2.0 inches/hour), the evaluation is absolutely false and the restrictive feature is not poor effulent filter field.

If no data is entered, then an artificial default value(s) is used.

Ames Description Prior to 1996
 ___________________________________________________________________
                       |             LIMITS             |RESTRICTIVE
+                       ________________________________
     PROPERTY          |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
                       |          |          |          |
+___________________________________________________________________
 
 2.  PERMEABILITY           ---      2.0-6.0     >6.0    POOR FILTER
     (0-60", IN/HR)
  
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
The values given on the Soils-5 for permeability are examined and a low value for each layer is determined.  The low value used for comparison depends on which of the following conditions is met first. If no data is entered, then an artificial value of 100 is used.  If the entry is of the form '<xx', then an artificial value of 0 is used.  Otherwise the low value is used.
 
The layers within the given depths are examined.  The surface layers are each rated separately.  The lowest value found from all the sublayers is rated.  The rating algorithm used is as follows:
 
   A value >= 6.0 gets a SEVERE rating.
   A value >= 2.0 and < 6.0 gets a MODERATE rating.
 
If the sublayer rating is SEVERE, then this property is rated SEVERE and no phasing will be done, regardless of the surface layer ratings.
 
If the sublayer rating is MODERATE, then this property is rated MODERATE if there is any SLIGHT or MODERATE surface layer rating, and it is rated SEVERE if there is any SEVERE surface layer rating.  Phasing will be done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks for the maximum electrical conductivity present in the 0-5 cm layer and indexes the degree to which electrical conductivity presents a salinization risk.
Where the soil property "EC MAXIMUM, 0-5 CM (ND)" is:

     >= 8 mmhos/cm            the soil is limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 1.0.
     >  2.001 and < 8 mmhos/cm    the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number between 0 and 1.0.
     <= 2.001 mmhos/cm            the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

Logic: 
Identify existing salinity as a risk to germination of plant seeds.

Reference:
Eilers, R.G., Eilers, W.D., Fitzgerald, M.M., 1997, A Salinity Risk Index for Soils of the Canadian Prairies : Hydrology Journal, v. 5, no. 1, p. 68-79.

Anderson, K., Zimmerman, D., Ulmer, M., 2010, Development and Application of a Salinity Risk Index for the Red River Valley of the North, MLRA 56.

This evaluation checks for the maximum electrical conductivity present in the 5-150 cm layer and indexes the degree to which electrical conductivity presents a salinization risk.
Where the soil property "EC MAXIMUM, 5-150 CM (ND)" is:

     >= 8 mmhos/cm             the soil is limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 1.0.
     >  2.001 and < 8 mmhos/cm     the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number between 0 and 1.0.
     <= 2.001 mmhos/cm             the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

Logic: 
Identify existing salinity in the 5-150 cm layer as a risk to survival of plants due to reduced osmotic pressure in the roots. Target salinity known to exist that has the potential to be carried to or near the surface via episaturation including associated capillary rise.

Reference:
Eilers, R.G., Eilers, W.D., Fitzgerald, M.M., 1997, A Salinity Risk Index for Soils of the Canadian Prairies : Hydrology Journal, v. 5, no. 1, p. 68-79.

Anderson, K., Zimmerman, D., Ulmer, M., 2010, Development and Application of a Salinity Risk Index for the Red River Valley of the North, MLRA 56.

Calculates the Mean Annual Precipitation minus the potential evapotranspiration using an equation as close to Hamon (1963) as was possible.  Result is mm frost free day.  Can be negative in dry climates. Where the soil property "MAP MINUS PET (HAMON), MM/ GROWING SEASON" is:
	>= 550 mm            the soil is limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 1.0.
    >  1 and < 550 mm    the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number between 0 and 1.0. 
	<  1                 the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation index is expressed as the number 0.

LOGIC:
Mean annual precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration expressed in mm/day multiplied by the number of frost free days equals the amount of surplus water in the soil profile during the growing season.

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

Reference: 
Hamon, W. R., 1963. Computation of direct runoff amounts from storm rainfall.  Int Assoc. Sci. Hydrol. Pub 63:52-62.

Eilers, R.G., Eilers, W.D., Fitzgerald, M.M., 1997, A Salinity Risk Index for Soils of the Canadian Prairies : Hydrology Journal, v. 5, no. 1, p. 68-79.

Note:
Ideally one would adjust the mean annual precipitation by subtracting precipitation that occurs during winter months when potential evapotraspiration is at or near 0. Frost free days are not an accurate portrail of the time period during which all evapotraspiration occurs, however, it is the best alternative available while using NASIS 6.4.1 and the data and interpretations generator available within the transactional database.
A logical assumption, in North Dakota, for most years is that evapotranspiration is 0 during the months of NOV, DEC, JAN, FEB, and MAR when soil water is typically frozen and plants are typically dormant.
propname: MAP MINUS PET (HAMON), MM/ GROWING SEASON

evalname: SRI - CaCO3 1 TO 5 IN DEPTH 0-50 & CLAY <= 18 (ND)
evaldesc:
The evaluation checks for clay contentent less than or equal to 18 percent and the presence of calcium carbonate in depth 0-50 cm where the taxonomic particle size class is either coarse-loamy, loamy-skeletal, sandy, or sandy-skeletal.  This index expresses the degree to which calcium carbonate presents a salinization risk.  
Where the soil property "CaCO3 IN DEPTH 0-50 CM & CLAY <= 18 (ND)" is:

	>= 5%           the soil is limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 1.0.
     > 1 and < 5%           the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number between 0 and 1.0. 
	<= 1%           the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 0.

LOGIC: 
Soil Taxonomy (Soil Survey Staff, 2014) was used as a proxy for estimating hydrology. According to Knuteson et al. (1989) and Redmond and McClelland (1959) upward soil water flux and evapotranspiration are responsible for the accumulation of carbonates in the soil profile and are considered evidence that these are discharge sites. This research infers more soluble salts responsible for salinization will move in the soil profile in a similar fashion. 

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

Reference:
Anderson, K., Zimmerman, D., Ulmer, M., 2010, Development and Application of a Salinity Risk Index for the Red River Valley of the North, MLRA 56.

Knuteson, J. A., J. L. Richardson, D. D. Patterson, and L. Prunty. 1989. Pedogenic carbonates in a
Calciaquoll associated with a recharge wetland. Soil Sci. Am. J. 53:495-499.

Redmond, C. E. and J. E. McClelland. 1959. Occurrence and distribution of lime in Calcium Carbonate
Solonchak and associated soils in eastern North Dakota. Soil Sci. Soc. Am. Proc. 23:61-65.

Soil Survey Staff. 2014. Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th edition.

evaldesc:
The De Martonne (1926) aridity index (Am) (as reviewed in Maliva and Missimer, 2012 and Lunga et al., 2011) uses temperature as a proxy for ETp as follows: Am = P/(T + 10) where, P (mm) is the annual precipitation and T (C) the annual mean temperature. The equation is appropriate for temperatures greater than -9.9C. The De Martonne aridity index decreases (approaches zero) with increasing aridity. Aridity index values greater the 30 are considered not fragile.

The shape of the scoring curve is sigmoid as follows:

	Aridity Index score = (a + cx + ex2)/(1 + bx + dx2)
	a = 0.99992575; b = -0.069544299; c = -0.065093715; d = 0.0019192058; e = 0.0010584767; x = aridity index

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks for the presence of bedrock within a specified depth.  The component data are check for restriction_kind = "bedrock (lithic)" or "bedrock (paralithic)" and restriction_depth_to_top is evaluated.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where the soil component property restriction_kind = "bedrock (lithic)" or "bedrock (paralithic)" and the restriction_depth_to_top is less than 91 then the evaluation is absolutely true and depth to bedrock is a restrictive feature.
     AND
  Where the soil component property restriction_kind = "bedrock (lithic)" or "bedrock (paralithic)" and the restriction_depth_to_top is equal to or greater than 120 cm then the evaluation is absolutely false and depth to bedrock is not a restrictive feature.

     AND

     PROPERTY          |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE

 Description of Calculation:

 The values given on the Soils-5 for depth to rock are examined and the low value determined.  The low value used for comparison depends on which of the following conditions is met first.

evaldesc:
Evaluates the property MAP MINUS POTENTIAL EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (HAMON) (ND) to determine if evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation. This condition allows salts to accumulate in the soil as they do not move vertically or laterally. A method for estimating potential evapotranspiration is described by Hamon (1963) is used to determine whether the climate generally facilitates leaching by subtracting the mean annual precipitation from the potential evapotranspiration.  When the precipitation deficit exceeds 100 mm the climate is considered to no longer cause leaching in most soils.   
   
Property evaluated: MAP MINUS POTENTIAL EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (HAMON) (ND)
               Leaching                   MAP-PET >= 10 mm/yr
               Transition                 MAP-PET -100 to 10 mm/yr
               Non-leaching            MAP-PET <= -100 mm/yr

Reference: Hamon, W. R., 1963. Computation of direct runoff amounts from storm rainfall.  Int Assoc. Sci. Hydrol. Pub 63:52-62.

evaldesc:
Rates components for presence of very firm or firmer consistence within 91cm.

This evaluation checks for moist consistence of very firm or extremely firm.  Moist consistence for all layers with top depth < 200cm are examined and those with very firm or extremely firm consistence are evaluated for depth.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where moist consistence is very firm or extremely firm and horizon top depth RV is less than 61cm (24 inches) the evaluation is absolutely true and CONSISTENCE is a restrictive feature.
   OR
  Where moist consistence is very firm or extremely firm and horizon top depth RV is greater than 91cm (36 inches) the evaluation is absolutely false and CONSISTENCE is not a restrictive feature.

If moist consistence within 91cm is null or is less firm than very firm, then the property assumption is that the component doesn't have a horizon with the required consistence.
propname: STS - VERY FIRM OR FIRMER CONSISTENCE - TEST (OH)

evaldesc: If a fragipan is between 61 and 91cm (24 and 36 inches) then there may not be sufficient vertical separation distance to meet OH STS rules. If a fragipan is less than 61cm then this is absolutely true and the fuzzy rating is 1.0.

This evaluation checks for platy structure.  Structure group for all layers with top depth < 200cm are examined and those with *platy* are evaluated for depth.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where structure group is *platy* and horizon top depth RV is less than 61cm (24 inches) BUT NOT 0 the evaluation is absolutely true and PLATY STRUCTURE is a restrictive feature.
   OR
  Where structure group is *platy*  and horizon top depth RV is greater than 91cm (36 inches) the evaluation is absolutely false and PLATY STRUCTURE is not a restrictive feature.

If structure group within 91cm is null or is not *platy*, then the property assumption is that the component doesn't have a horizon with the required structure.

evaldesc:
This evaluation checks the greater than 3 inch fraction of the soil.  The weighted average of the component horizon rock_frag_3_to_10_in and rock_frag_greater_than_10_in is calculated for the 0 to 100 cm (40in) depth of the soil and the result is checked and evaluated.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:

  Where the total of each layers weighted average of the soil component horizon properties rock_frag_3_to_10_in and rock_frag_greater_than_10_in from 0 to a depth of 100cm (40in) less than 25% the evaluation is absolutely false and "LARGE STONES" is not a restrictive feature.

If no data is entered, then a default value of 0 is used.

                                                  |                             LIMITS                            |  RESTRICTIVE
     PROPERTY                     |  SLIGHT  | MODERATE |  SEVERE  |  FEATURE
 9. 1/FRACTION >3 IN       <25                25-50                    >50            LARGE STONES
      (WT PCT)        
 
 Description of Calculation:
+___________________________
 
 The values given on the Soils-5 for fraction 3-10 inches are examined and a high value for each layer is determined.  The high value used in the calculation depends on which of the following conditions is met first.
 
 If a single value of '99' is entered, then an artificial value of 100 is used.
 
 If a single value not equal to '99' is entered, then an artificial value of 0 is used.
 
 Otherwise the high value is used.
 
 A separate weighted average to 40 inches is calculated for each surface layer.
 
           A weighted average > 50 gets a SEVERE rating.
           A weighted average > 25 and <= 50 gets a MODERATE rating.
           A weighted average <= 25 gets a SLIGHT rating.

Evaluates the weighted average electrical conductivity in the 0-5 cm layer and indexes the degree to which electrical conductivity presents a salinization risk.
Where the soil property "BULK EC 0-5CM MAX OR ABOVE RESTRICTION (ND)" is:

     <= 0 mmhos/cm            the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 0.

Logic: 
Salinization in the 0-5 cm layer influences germination and impacts the establishment of vegetative cover.

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

Reference:
Eilers, R.G., Eilers, W.D., Fitzgerald, M.M., 1997, A Salinity Risk Index for Soils of the Canadian Prairies : Hydrology Journal, v. 5, no. 1, p. 68-79.

Anderson, K., Zimmerman, D., Ulmer, M., 2010, Development and Application of a Salinity Risk Index for the Red River Valley of the North, MLRA 56.

evaldesc:
Evaluates the weighted average electrical conductivity in the 0-150 cm layer and indexes the degree to which electrical conductivity presents a salinization risk.
Where the soil property "BULK EC 5-150CM MAX OR ABOVE RESTRICTION (ND)" is:

     >= 8 mmhos/cm                the soil is limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 1.0.
     >  0 and < 8 mmhos/cm    the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as a number between 0 and 1.0.
     <= 0 mmhos/cm                the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 0.

Logic: 
Identify existing salinity in the 5-150 cm layer as a risk to survival of plants. It is known that the osmotic pressure gradient between plant roots and the soil solution results in a negative impact on plant performance resembling drought stress. Target salinity known to exist that has the potential to be carried to or near the surface via episaturation including associated capillary rise.

SRI = Salinity Risk Index

evaldesc:
Some surfaces are shaped so as to gather water.  This additional water can lead to erosion if the soil is impervious or excessive leaching if the soil is permeable.
The soil surface and subsurface must generally concentrate water flow.  Research has shown that in regions where rainfall is limited the concave parts of the landscape also concentrate subsurface water flow as well as surface flow.  The shape of the land surface curvature in the up-down and across directions is considered.  The shape can be convex, linear, or concave in both the up and down or across orientations.  Areas that are concave up-down and linear across are the best at concentrating salts at the soil surface.  This basically describes the footslopes of stream channels.  
Where the soil property "SALINIZATION WATER GATHERING SURFACE (ND)" is:

               0.0                  Least concentrating         convex up-down and convex across
               >0 and <1.0  Transition                         all others
               >= 1.0           Best salt concentrator     concave updown and linear across

Evaluates the persistence of the seasonal high water table during the growing season as it relates to salinization risk. Salts become mobile in soil when they are dissolved in the soil water and they accumulate in the soil as the soil water evaporates or dries.  Most soil water movement happens when the soil is saturated, thus, the depth to saturation and its temporal persistence influence whether salts will remain deep in the profile or be carried to the surface.  If the water table remains deep the salts will accumulate deeper in the profile.  If the water table is close enough to the surface that capillary rise and evapotranspiration can bring water to the soil surface and salts will accumulate at the surface as the soil water evaporates. 

Property evaluated: WATER TABLE W/IN 100CM  MONTHS DURING GROWING SEASON (ND)

Persistent water table                      >4 months per year           the soil is not limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 0.
Somewhat persistent water table    1 to 3 months per year       the soil is somewhat limited and the degree of limitation is expressed a number between 0 and 1.0. 
Non-persistent water table               0 months per year             the soil is limited and the degree of limitation is expressed as the number 1.0.

 15/100 minus % passing No. 4 sieve > 25.
 16/100 minus % passing No. 4 sieve < 25.

 According to footnote 12, calculations are done for both the thickest layer and the bottom layer.

 Description of Calculation for Thickest Layer:
______________________________________________

 The layer with the most inches between 10 and 60 inches is determined.  This could be a surface layer or a sublayer.  The unified values given on the Soils-5 are examined for the appropriate layer(s).

 The layer(s) being examined are rated according to the following algorithm:

 If GW, GP, GW-GM, or GP-GM is listed as a unified entry, or if SW, SP, SW-SM or SP-SM is listed as a unified entry and footnote 15 applies (see following description of footnote 15), then a PROBABLE rating is given.

 Otherwise an IMPROBABLE rating is given.

 If the thickest layer is a sublayer, then this property is rated the same as this sublayer's rating.

 If the thickest layer is a surface layer, then this property is rated PROBABLE if there is any PROBABLE surface layer rating.  If there is none, then it is rated IMPROBABLE.

 Restrictive feature terms are assigned appropriately.


 Description of Calculation for Bottom Layer:
____________________________________________

 If the bottom layer has no data, then this calculation is skipped and the ratings for the thickest layer are chosen.

 Otherwise, this calculation is the same as that for the thickest layer, except it is done for the bottom layer.  The bottom layer, like the thickest layer, may be a surface layer or a sublayer.


 Calculations for Footnotes 15 and 16
____________________________________

 To do the calculations for these footnotes, the values given on the Soils-5 for % passing No. 4 sieve are examined.

 % passing No. 4 sieve
_____________________

 Assign values to No_4_Lo and No_4_Hi.

 If no data is entered, then No_4_Lo = 0 and No_4_Hi = 0.

 If a single value, say x, is entered, then No_4_Lo = x and  No_4_Hi = x.

 If the entry is a normal range, say x-y, then No_4_Lo = x and  No_4_Hi = y.

 Once these values have been assigned, the following calculations take place.

 100 - No_4_Lo = Lo
 100 - No_4_Hi = Hi

 maximum(Lo,Hi) = max

 If max > 25 then footnote 15 applies.
 If max <= 25 then footnote 16 applies.

 For Property No. 2, UNIFIED, the best ratings must be chosen between those calculated for the thickest layer and the bottom layer.

 If both the thickest and bottom layers are rated PROBABLE, then the bottom layer is chosen.

 If the thickest layer is rated PROBABLE and the bottom layer is rated IMPROBABLE, then the thickest layer is chosen.

 If the bottom layer is rated PROBABLE and the thickest layer is rated IMPROBABLE, then the bottom layer is chosen.

 If neither the thickest or bottom layer is rated PROBABLE, then they must both be rated IMPROBABLE and the bottom layer is chosen.

 If the ratings for the thickest layer were chosen, then the calculations on the following page for Property No. 3, LAYER THICKNESS, are done.

 If a single value of '99' is entered, then an artificial value of 100 is used.

 If a single value not equal to '99' is entered, then an artificial  value of 0 is used.

 Otherwise the high value is used.

 If surface layers are not included, then a weighted average from 10 to 60 inches is calculated and rated.  No phasing is done.

 If surface layers are included, then a separate weighted average from 10 to 60 inches is calculated and rated for each surface layer. Phasing will be done using texture terms if more than one rating is given.

    A weighted average > 50 gets an IMPROBABLE rating.

 Description of Calculation for Bottom Layer:
____________________________________________

 Calculations for Footnotes 15 and 16
____________________________________

 To do the calculations for these footnotes, the values given on the Soils-5 for % passing No. 4 sieve are examined.

 % passing No. 4 sieve
_____________________

 Assign values to No_4_Lo and No_4_Hi.

 If no data is entered, then No_4_Lo = 0 and No_4_Hi = 0.

 If a single value, say x, is entered, then No_4_Lo = x and  No_4_Hi = x.

 If the entry is a normal range, say x-y, then No_4_Lo = x and  No_4_Hi = y.

 Once these values have been assigned, the following calculations take place.

 100 - No_4_Lo = Lo
 100 - No_4_Hi = Hi

 maximum(Lo,Hi) = max

 If max > 25 then footnote 15 applies.
 If max <= 25 then footnote 16 applies.

 If the bottom layer is rated PROBABLE and the thickest layer is rated IMPROBABLE, then the bottom layer is chosen.

 If neither the thickest or bottom layer is rated PROBABLE, then they must both be rated IMPROBABLE and the bottom layer is chosen.

evaldesc:
This evaluation averages the low, rv, and high depths for all months that have consecutive "wet" soil moisture status.

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition:
  Where average of soil_moisture_depth_top for all consecutive months (comonth.month) where soil property soil_moisture_status equals "wet" is =<60cm, then the evaluation returns a value greater than 0.

The criteria was rated based on the following breaks:
Well Suited 5.5-7.8
Moderately Suited - 7.8-8.0, 4.5-5.5
Poorly Suited - >8.0, <5.5

The fuzzy space is defined as the condition: 
Where the soil property  frag3to10_r is null for all rows in the chorizon table, the property returns a value of 0.  If frag3to10_r is not null, a value of 1 is returned.  This is done to make components lacking horizon data return a 0 and so be "not assighned".

Duripans that are moderately deep are common in slickspots but not always present.

A soil with a duripan within 75 cm of the soil surface is well suited

Assigns a numerical rating by MLRA for the Idaho Slickspot Site Suitability.  Slickspot peppergrass (Lepidium papilliferum) has been documented across SW Idaho.  It is theorized the full extent of suitable sites could trickle across political boundaries into Southeast Oregon and Northeast Nevada. Landform is remnant Pleistocene lakebeds or playas, theseslightly  concave microsites are found on terraces or lava plateaus. Elevations from 2,200-3,300 feet mostly in the Snake River Plain, full extent maybe more like 2,000-5,000ft.  In Idaho the best sites are found in MLRAs 11 and 25, it maybe possible in the far lower end of 10 adjacent to 11 but would not be ideal conditions.


MLRA 11, 25 well suited
MLRA 23,24 suited
MLRA 10,12, 13 poorly suited
MLRA 43 not suited

>70% is poorly suited
20-70% is suited
